children: By Meghan Bobrowsky, Laura J. Nelson and Paul Kiernan
A proposed billionaire tax had Mark Zuckerberg thinking about leaving California. Provisions around the 2-for-1 split of Meta Platforms' stock are designed to keep him in the state.

The company said in a filing Wednesday that Zuckerberg, Meta's chief executive officer, has agreed to maintain primary residence in the same state as the company's headquarters for the next eight years, barring "material unforeseen circumstances." Zuckerberg had told Meta board members he was evaluating whether to leave the state in response to a proposed first-of-its-kind wealth tax set to go before California voters on Nov. 3, according to the filing.

If the tax becomes law, Zuckerberg would owe a "significant, multi-billion dollar tax payment" based on his Meta shares, the company said in the filing. Meta said Zuckerberg's tax bill could force a share sale that would reduce his voting interest from 60.6% to 53% or lower.

During its earnings report Wednesday, Meta announced the creation of a new class of nonvoting stock to fund its continued artificial-intelligence expansion, to be issued to existing shareholders as a dividend. To align Zuckerberg's interest with the company's, his new shares will be "stapled" to the original ones, preventing him from selling them without also selling his voting shares. The shares will be gradually released from stapling over a period of eight years according to a preset schedule.

But the company also said this "Founder Alignment Agreement" wouldn't cover all of Zuckerberg's new shares. Zuckerberg will be able to immediately sell up to 20% of his new Class C shares, representing 10% of his financial stake in Meta, "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law."

"Mr. Zuckerberg's continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company's headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry," the company said, adding that it wanted to ensure Zuckerberg "remains working closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs."
In the filing, the company said it wanted to avoid the challenges encountered during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg wasn't working from the same location as the management team.

Proposition 40, proposed by a healthcare union, would levy a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of California residents with net assets of $1 billion or more. Its novel approach — taxing assets, rather than income — has prompted some of the state's wealthiest residents to consider moves to lower-tax states, including Florida and Texas.

The proposed wealth tax would apply to billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, and would be based on net worth as of Dec. 31 of this year. Unlike traditional taxes on income or real estate, it would apply to financial assets — including unrealized capital gains on stocks — as well as art, intellectual property and other holdings.

The proposal has sparked anxiety among wealthy Californians that, even if voters reject this wealth tax, others could follow. The state depends on high earners to pay for basic services; in 2023, more than one-sixth of the state's personal income tax revenue came from the top 0.1% of earners, or about 17,500 filers.

But proving that you've left California isn't simple. The state's famously dogged auditors have no hard-and-fast test to establish residency, relying instead on 19 factors — which can include credit-card transactions, gym memberships and doctors' appointments — to verify if wealthy taxpayers who claim to have left the state are telling the truth.
